모든 앱**을 다룰 수 있다는 것이 장점입니다. 반면 좌표와 시각 판단에 의존하기 때문에 느리고, 화면 배율·창 위치·레이아웃 변화에 취약하며, 매 단계 스크린샷을 모델이 처리해야 합니다. Computer Use 관련 스킬들도 웹 작업에는 Playwright나 CDP를 우선하고 GUI 전용 작업에서만 Computer Use를 쓰도록 권장합니다. citeturn623610view1turn623610view3\n\nego-lite는 기본적으로 다음처럼 동작합니다.\n\n```text\n의미 기반 페이지 Snapshot\n  ↓\n역할·텍스트·locator로 요소 탐색\n  ↓\nJavaScript 코드로 여러 동작 일괄 실행\n"}]},{"role":"user","content":[{"content_type":"text","text":"ruflo와 omc에서 mcp가 어떤 구조로 동작하고 있는지 궁금해."}]},{"role":"assistant","content":[{"content_type":"text","text":"# 핵심 차이\n\n두 프로젝트에서 MCP의 위치가 다릅니다.\n\n> **Ruflo의 MCP는 오케스트레이션 제어 평면에 가깝고,**  \n> **OMC의 MCP는 Claude Code에 기능을 공급하는 로컬 도구 브리지에 가깝습니다.**\n\n다만 Ruflo에서도 MCP가 직접 모든 코딩 에이전트 프로세스를 실행하는 것은 아닙니다. 현재 Claude Code용 Ruflo 스킬은 **MCP로 swarm의 토폴로지·상태·메모리를 초기화한 뒤, 실제 Claude 서브에이전트는 Claude Code의 네이티브 `Task` 도구로 실행**하도록 안내합니다. 즉, Ruflo MCP는 특히 **조정·상태·라우팅 계층**의 비중이 큽니다. citeturn748310search1turn748310search3\n\n반대로 OMC의 핵심 오케스트레이션은 다음 조합에서 일어납니다.\n\n```text\nHooks → Skills → Claude Code Task → State\n```\n\n기본 MCP 서버인 `t`는 상태, 메모리, LSP, AST, Python 실행기 같은 보조 기능을 제공하며, 서브에이전트를 어떤 순서로 실행할지는 주로 Hooks·Skills·Claude Code의 `Task`, 그리고 `omc team` CLI가 담당합니다. citeturn334981search0turn964632search2\n\n---\n\n# 1. 두 프로젝트에서 공통인 MCP 동작\n\n둘 다 기본적으로 Claude Code가 MCP 클라이언트이고, 프로젝트가 로컬 MCP 서버 프로세스를 띄우는 형태입니다.\n\n```text\nClaude Code\n    │\n    │ stdio\n    ▼\nNode.js / CLI 기반 MCP 서버\n    │\n    ├── 사용 가능한 도구 목록 제공\n    ├── JSON Schema 기반 인자 검증\n    ├── 도구 호출 실행\n    └── 결과 반환\n```\n\nLLM은 MCP 서버 내부에 들어 있는 것이 아닙니다. Claude가 판단하고, MCP 서버는 Claude가 호출할 수 있는 명시적인 함수 집합을 제공합니다.\n\nOMC는 루트 `.mcp.json`에서 `t`라는 서버 하나를 등록하며, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bridge/mcp-server.cjs`를 Node.js로 실행합니다. 브리지 소스는 `StdioServerTransport`를 사용합니다. citeturn964632search0turn250670view1\n\nRuflo도 전체 설치에서는 다음과 같은 프로세스형 MCP 서버를 등록합니다.\n\n```bash\nclaude mcp add ruflo -- npx ruflo@latest mcp start\n```\n\n중요하게도 Ruflo는 **플러그인만 설치한 경우 MCP 서버가 등록되지 않고**, 전체 `ruflo init` 경로를 사용해야 MCP 서버, Hooks, daemon 등이 함께 활성화됩니다. MCP가 없으면 `memory_store`, `swarm_init`, `agent_spawn` 같은 도구를 Claude가 호출할 수 없습니다. citeturn748310search6\n\n---\n\n# 2. Ruflo의 MCP 구조\n\n## 전체 구조\n\nRuflo의 문서상 아키텍처는 대략 다음 형태입니다.\n\n```text\nClaude Code / Codex / Web UI / CLI\n                  │\n                  │ MCP 도구 호출\n                  ▼\n┌───────────────────────────────────────┐\n│             Ruflo MCP Server          │\n│                                       │\n│  Tool Registry                        │\n│  ├── swarm_*                          │\n│  ├── agent_*                          │\n│  ├── task_*                  "}]}],"diff":null}}

합니다.\n\n```text\n1. 공통 워크플로우 구축\n2. 역할별 계약 통합\n3. 명시적 또는 추천형 라우팅\n4. 결과 데이터 축적\n5. 검증된 작업만 자동 라우팅\n```\n\n---\n\n# 왜 처음부터 완전 자동 분담하면 안 되는가\n\n## 1. 작업 유형은 시작할 때보다 진행 중에 바뀌는 경우가 많습니다\n\n예를 들어 처음에는 단순한 라우터를 만들면, 실제 개발 하네스보다 라우터 유지보수에 더 많은 시간을 쓰게 될 수 있습니다.\n\n---\n\n## 2. 두 모델의 워크플로우를 별도로 관리하면 반드시 드리프트가 생깁니다\n\n예를 들어 처음에는 양쪽에 모두 다음 규칙이 있었다고 가정하겠습니다.\n\n```text\n- 구현 전 PRD 확인\n- 변경 전 영향 범위 분석\n- 테스트 Claude가 판단하고, MCP 서버는 Claude가 호출할 수 있는 명시적인 함수 집합을 제공합니다.\n\nOMC는 루트 `.mcp.json`에서 `t`라는 서버 하나를 등록하며, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bridge/mcp-server.cjs`를 Node.js로 실행합니다. 브리지 소스는 `StdioServerTransport`를 사용합니다. citeturn964632search0turn250670view1\n\nRuflo도 전체 설치에서는 다음과 같은 프로세스형 MCP 서버를 등록합니다.\n\n```bash\nclaude mcp add ruflo -- npx ruflo@latest mcp start\n```\n\n중요하게도 Ruflo는 **플러그인만 설치한 경우 MCP 서버가 등록되지 않고**, 전체 `ruflo init` 경로를 사용해야 MCP 서버, Hooks, daemon 등이 함께 활성화됩니다. Over time, individual workflows will expose more targeted customization points tailored to what that workflow actually does — things like step-specific toggles, stage flags, output template paths, or review gates. ... To change an install answer durably, re-run the installer (it remembers your prior answers as defaults) or shadow the value in `_bmad/custom/config.toml`. ...   * Run the `bmad-customize` skill — it enumerates every customizable skill installed in your project, shows which ones already have overrides, and walks you through adding or updating one\n\n# How to Customize BMad\n\nTailor agent personas, inject domain context, add capabilities, and configure workflow behavior — all without modifying installed files. Your customizations survive every update.\n\nDon’t want to hand-author TOML? Use `bmad-customize`\n\nThe `bmad-customize` skill is a guided authoring helper for the per-skill agent/workflow override surface described in this doc. It scans what’s customizable in your installation, helps you choose the right surface (agent vs workflow) for your intent, writes the override file for you, and verifies the merge landed. Central-config overrides (`_bmad/custom/config.toml`) are out of scope for v1 — hand-author those per the Central Configuration section below. Run the skill whenever you want to make a per-skill change; this doc is the reference for what each surface exposes and how merging works.\n\n## When to Use This\n\nSection titled “When to Use This”\n\n  * You want to change an agent’s personality or communication style\n  * You need to give an agent persistent facts to recall (e.g. “our org is AWS-only”)\n  * You want to add procedural startup steps the agent must run every session\n  * You want to add custom menu items that trigger your own skills or prompts\n  * Your team needs shared customizations committed to git, with personal preferences layered on top\n\nPrerequisites\n\n  * BMad installed in your project (see How to Install BMad)\n  * A way to run the resolver script — BMad is standardizing on `uv` (`uv run`, which provisions Python for you); a plain `python3` 3.11+ on your PATH still works during the transition. The script uses only stdlib `tomllib`, so there’s nothing to `pip install`.\n  * A text editor for TOML files\n\n## How It Works\n\nSection titled “How It Works”\n\nEvery customizable skill ships a `customize.toml` file with its defaults. This file defines the skill’s complete customization surface — read it to see what’s customizable. You never edit this file. Instead, you create sparse override files containing only the fields you want to change.\n\n### Three-Layer Override Model\n## Steps\n\nSection titled “Steps”\n\n### 1. Find the Skill’s Customization Surface\n\nSection titled “1. Find the Skill’s Customization Surface”\n\nLook at the skill’s `customize.toml` in its installed directory. For example, the PM agent:\n    \n    `\n    \n    .claude/skills/bmad-agent-pm/customize.toml\n    \n    `\n\n(Path varies by IDE — Cursor uses `.cursor/skills/`, Cline uses `.cline/skills/`, and so on.)\n\nThis file is the canonical schema. Every field you see is customizable (excluding the read-only identity fields noted above).\n\n### 2. Create Your Override File\n\nSection titled “2. Create Your Override File”\n\nCreate the `_bmad/custom/` directory in your project root if it doesn’t exist. Then create a file named after the skill:\n    \n    `\n    \n    _bmad/custom/\n    \n      bmad-agent-pm.toml        # team overrides (committed to git)\n    \n      bmad-agent-pm.user.toml   # personal preferences (gitignored)\n    \n    `\n\nDo NOT copy the whole `customize.toml`\n\nOverride files are sparse. Include only the fields you’re changing — nothing else. Every field you omit is inherited automatically from the layer below (team from defaults, user from team-or-defaults).\n\nCopying the full `customize.toml` into an override is actively harmful: the next update ships new defaults, but your override file locks in the old values. You’ll silently drift out of sync with every release.\n\nExample — changing the icon and adding one principle:\n\n_bmad/custom/bmad-agent-pm.toml\n    \n    `\n    \n    # Just the fields I'm changing. Everything else inherits.\n    \n    \n    \n    \n    [agent]\n    \n    icon = \"🏥\"\n    \n    principles = [\n    \n      \"Ship nothing that can't pass an FDA audit.\",\n    \n    ]\n    \n    `\n\nThis appends the new principle to the defaults (leaving the shipped principles intact) and replaces the icon. Every other field stays as shipped.\n\n### 3. Customize What You Need\n\nSection titled “3. Customize What You Need”\n\nAll examples below assume BMad’s flat agent schema. Fields live directly under `[agent]` — no nested `metadata` or `persona` sub-tables.\n## How Resolution Works\n\nSection titled “How Resolution Works”\n\nOn activation, the agent’s SKILL.md runs a shared Python script that does the three-layer merge and returns the resolved block as JSON. The script uses only the Python standard library’s `tomllib` module (no external dependencies). BMad is standardizing on `uv run` to invoke these scripts (uv provisions a suitable Python for you); a plain `python3` still works during the transition:\n\nTerminal window\n    \n    `\n    \n    uv run {project-root}/_bmad/scripts/resolve_customization.py \\\n    \n      --skill {skill-root} \\\n    \n      --key agent\n    \n    `\n\nRequirements: Python 3.11+ (earlier versions don’t include `tomllib`); nothing to `pip install`. Running via `uv run` is the going-forward standard — uv resolves a suitable interpreter for you. If you run it with `python3` directly during the transition, check your version with `python3 --version`: some platforms (macOS without Homebrew, Ubuntu 22.04) default `python3` to 3.10 or earlier, so you may need to install 3.11+ separately.\n\n`--skill` points at the skill’s installed directory (where `customize.toml` lives). The skill name is derived from the directory’s basename, and the script looks up `_bmad/custom/{skill-name}.toml` and `{skill-name}.user.toml` automatically.\n\nUseful invocations:\n\nTerminal window\n    \n    `\n    \n    # Resolve the full agent block\n    \n    uv run {project-root}/_bmad/scripts/resolve_customization.py \\\n    \n      --skill /abs/path/to/bmad-agent-pm \\\n    \n      --key agent\n    \n    \n    \n    \n    # Resolve a single field\n    \n    uv run {project-root}/_bmad/scripts/resolve_customization.py \\\n    \n      --skill /abs/path/to/bmad-agent-pm \\\n    \n      --key agent.icon\n    \n    \n    \n    \n    # Full dump\n    \n    uv run {project-root}/_bmad/scripts/resolve_customization.py \\\n    \n      --skill /abs/path/to/bmad-agent-pm\n    \n    `\n\nOutput is always JSON. If the script is unavailable on a given platform, the SKILL.md tells the agent to read the three TOML files directly and apply the same merge rules.\n\n## Workflow Customization\n## Central Configuration\n\nSection titled “Central Configuration”\n\nPer-skill `customize.toml` covers deep behavior (hooks, menus, persistent_facts, persona overrides for a single agent or workflow). A separate surface covers cross-cutting state — install answers and the agent roster that external skills like `bmad-party-mode`, `bmad-retrospective`, and `bmad-advanced-elicitation` consume. That surface lives in four TOML files at project root:\n    \n    `\n    \n    _bmad/config.toml               (installer-owned)  team scope:   install answers + agent roster\n    \n    _bmad/config.user.toml          (installer-owned)  user scope:   user_name, language, skill level\n    \n    _bmad/custom/config.toml        (human-authored)   team overrides (committed to git)\n    \n    _bmad/custom/config.user.toml   (human-authored)   personal overrides (gitignored)\n    \n    `\n\n### Four-Layer Merge\n\nSection titled “Four-Layer Merge”\n    \n    `\n    \n    Priority 1 (wins): _bmad/custom/config.user.toml\n    \n    Priority 2:        _bmad/custom/config.toml\n    \n    Priority 3:        _bmad/config.user.toml\n    \n    Priority 4 (base): _bmad/config.toml\n    \n    `\n\nSame structural rules as per-skill customize (scalars override, tables deep-merge, `code`/`id`-keyed arrays merge by key, other arrays append).\n\n### What Lives Where\n\nSection titled “What Lives Where”\n\nThe installer partitions answers by the `scope:` declared on each prompt in `module.yaml`:\n\n  * `[core]` and `[modules.<code>]` sections — install answers. Scope `team` lands in `_bmad/config.toml`; scope `user` lands in `_bmad/config.user.toml`.\n  * `[agents.<code>]` — agent essence (code, name, title, icon, description, team) distilled from each module’s `module.yaml` `agents:` block. Always team-scoped.\n\n### Editing Rules\n\nSection titled “Editing Rules”\n\n  * `_bmad/config.toml` and `_bmad/config.user.toml` are regenerated every install from the answers collected during the installer flow. Treat them as read-only outputs — direct edits will be overwritten on the next install. To change an install answer durably, re-run the installer (it remembers your prior answers as defaults) or shadow the value in `_bmad/custom/config.toml`.\n  * `_bmad/custom/config.toml` and `_bmad/custom/config.user.toml` are never touched by the installer. This is the correct surface for custom agents, agent descriptor overrides, team-enforced settings, and any value you want to pin regardless of install answers.\n\n### Example — Rebrand an Agent\n\nSection titled “Example — Rebrand an Agent”\n    \n    `\n    \n    # _bmad/custom/config.toml (committed to git, applies to every developer)\n    \n    \n    \n    \n    [agents.bmad-agent-pm]\n    \n    description = \"Healthcare PM — regulatory-aware, stakeholder-driven, FDA-shaped questions first.\"\n    \n    icon = \"🏥\"\n    \n    `\n\nThe resolver merges over the installer-written `[agents.bmad-agent-pm]`. `bmad-party-mode` and any other roster consumer pick up the new description automatically.\n\n### Example — Add a Fictional Agent\n\nSection titled “Example — Add a Fictional Agent”\n## Worked Examples\n\nSection titled “Worked Examples”\n\nFor enterprise-oriented recipes (shaping an agent across every workflow it dispatches, enforcing org conventions, publishing outputs to Confluence and Jira, customizing the agent roster, and swapping in your own output templates), see How to Expand BMad for Your Organization.\n\n## Troubleshooting\n\nSection titled “Troubleshooting”\n\nCustomization not appearing?\n\n  * Verify your file is in `_bmad/custom/` with the correct skill name\n  * Check TOML syntax: strings must be quoted, table headers use `[section]`, array-of-tables use `[[section]]`, and any scalar or array keys for a table must appear before any of that table’s `[[subtables]]` in the file\n  * For agents, customization lives under `[agent]` — fields written below that header belong to `agent` until another table header begins\n  * Remember `agent.name` and `agent.title` are read-only; overrides there have no effect\n\nUpdates broke my customization?\n\n  * Did you copy the full `customize.toml` into your override file? Don’t. Override files should contain only the fields you’re changing. A full copy locks in old defaults and silently drifts every release. Trim your override back to just the deltas.\n\nNeed to see what’s customizable?\n\n  * Run the `bmad-customize` skill — it enumerates every customizable skill installed in your project, shows which ones already have overrides, and walks you through adding or updating one\n  * Or read the skill’s `customize.toml` directly — every field there is customizable (except `name` and `title`)\n\nNeed to reset?\n\n  * Delete your override file from `_bmad/custom/` — the skill falls back to its built-in defaults--------------------------------------------------------------------------------\nGitHub - bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD: Breakthrough Method for Agile Ai Driven Development · GitHub (https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-method)\nciteturn0search2 [wordlim: 200] Published: 2 months ago; Crawled: 2 months ago; bmad-code-org / BMAD-METHOD Public ...   * GitHub Issues — Bug reports and feature requests\n\nbmad-code-org / BMAD-METHOD Public\n\n  * ### Uh oh!\n\nThere was an error while loading. The exact path depends on which IDE you selected during installation.\n\n| IDE / CLI | Skills directory |\n| --- | --- |\n| Claude Code | `.claude/skills/` |\n| Cursor | `.agents/skills/` |\n| Windsurf | `.agents/skills/` |\n| Other IDEs | See the installer output for the target path |\n\nEach skill is a directory containing a `SKILL.md` file. Valid values: stable | next.\n# Omit to inherit the installer's hardcoded default (stable).\n#\n# deprecated (optional, default false) — when true, the module is hidden from\n# the installer picker UNLESS it is already installed (so existing users can\n# still see/manage it, but new users are not offered it).\n# deprecation-message (optional) — surfaced in the picker hint for a deprecated\n# module that is still installed; use it to point users to the replacement.\n#\n# marketplace-plugin (optional, default false) — when true, the module's\n# installable skills are resolved from its .claude-plugin/marketplace.json via\n# the plugin resolver (instead of copying the single module-definition dir).\n# Use this for modules whose module.yaml does not sit alongside the skill\n# folders. module-definition should still point at the real module.yaml so\n# config/version lookups work.\n#\n# post-install-message (optional) — an \"action needed\" notice shown to the user\n# after install completes, once for each install run that includes the module.\n# Interactive installs require the user to acknowledge it (press Enter);\n# non-interactive (--yes) installs print it and continue. Use for required\n# follow-up steps (e.g. \"run the X setup skill\").\n#\n# aliases (optional) — prior `code` values this module was registered under.\n# An existing install recorded under an alias resolves to this entry (source,\n# name, description, post-install message) instead of being orphaned as\n# \"no source available\" when the code changes. quick-update also migrates the\n# install to the new code and removes the stale `_bmad/<alias>/` directory.\n\nmodules:\n  bmad-builder:\n    url: https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-builder\n    module-definition: skills/module.yaml\n    code: bmb\n    name: \"BMad Builder\"\n    description: \"Skill, workflow, and agent builder\"\n    defaultSelected: false\n    type: bmad-org\n    npmPackage: bmad-builder\n    default_channel: stable\n\n  bmad-creative-intelligence-suite:\n    url: https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-module-creative-intelligence-suite\n    module-definition: src/module.yaml\n    code: cis\n    name: \"BMad Creative Intelligence Suite\"\n    description: \"Creative thinking partners\"\n    defaultSelected: false\n    type: bmad-org\n    npmPackage: bmad-creative-intelligence-suite\n    default_channel: stable\n\n  bmad-method-test-architecture-enterprise:\n    url: https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-method-test-architecture-enterprise\n    module-definition: src/module.yaml\n    code: tea\n    name: \"BMad Test Architect\"\n    description: \"Enterprise testing BMM add-on\"\n    defaultSelected: false\n    type: bmad-org\n    npmPackage: bmad-method-test-architecture-enterprise\n    default_channel: stable\n\n  bmad-loop:\n    url: https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-loop\n    module-definition: src/bmad_loop/data/skills/bmad-loop-setup/assets/module.yaml\n    code: bmad-loop\n    # bauto is the pre-rename code (module was bmad-auto before both the repo\n    # and its contents were renamed to bmad-loop); keeps existing bauto\n    # installs migrating forward instead of being orphaned.\n    aliases: [bauto]\n    name: \"BMad Loop\"\n    description: \"Builds, verifies, and retros a whole epic unattended\"\n    defaultSelected: false\n    type: bmad-org\n    default_channel: stable\n    # Skills live outside a single module.yaml dir; To finish setup, run the bmad-loop-setup skill\n      from your agent:\n\n        > use the bmad-loop-setup skill\n\n      It installs the bmad-loop orchestrator tool and wires up the per-project\n      hooks and policy. The automation skills don't run until setup completes.\n\n  bmad-game-dev-studio:\n    url: https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-module-game-dev-studio.git\n    module-definition: src/module.yaml\n    code: gds\n    name: \"BMad Game Dev Studio\"\n    description: \"Ideate, design, and build games\"\n    defaultSelected: false\n    type: bmad-org\n    npmPackage: bmad-game-dev-studio\n    default_channel: stable\n\n  # --- Deprecated: hidden from the picker unless already installed ---\n\n  bmad-automator:\n    url: https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-automator\n    module-definition: skills/module.yaml\n    code: automator\n    name: \"BMad Automator Epic Builder Experimental\"\n    description: \"EXPERIMENTAL: only supports claude and codex currently\"\n    defaultSelected: false\n    type: experimental\n    npmPackage: bmad-story-automator\n    default_channel: next\n    deprecated: true\n    deprecation-message: \"BMad Automator has been deprecated and is replaced by BMad Loop (bmad-loop). Install BMad Loop instead.\"\n\n  bmad-method-wds-expansion:\n    url: https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-method-wds-expansion\n    module-definition: src/module.yaml\n    code: wds\n    plugin_name: bmad-wds # WDS marketplace.json declares the plugin under this name\n    name: \"Whiteport Design Studio\"\n    description: \"Strategic UX and Design first planning methodology\"\n    defaultSelected: false\n    type: bmad-org\n    npmPackage: bmad-wds\n    default_channel: stable\n    deprecated: true\n    deprecation-message: \"Whiteport Design Studio is no longer receiving updates. Its capabilities are being folded into BMad Method (bmm) as enhanced UX features. Your existing install is kept as-is.\"\n---\ntitle: Official Modules\ndescription: Add-on modules for building custom agents, creative intelligence, game development, and testing\nsidebar:\n  order: 5\n---\n\nBMad extends through official modules that you select during installation. These add-on modules provide specialized agents, workflows, and tasks for specific domains beyond the built-in core and BMM (Agile suite).\n\n:::tip[Installing Modules]\nRun `npx bmad-method install` and select the modules you want. The installer handles downloading, configuration, and IDE integration automatically.\n:::\n\n## BMad Builder\n\nCreate custom agents, workflows, and domain-specific modules with guided assistance. BMad Builder is the meta-module for extending the framework itself.\n\n- **Code:** `bmb`\n- **npm:** [`bmad-builder`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/bmad-builder)\n- **GitHub:** [bmad-code-org/bmad-builder](https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-builder)\n\n**Provides:**\n\n- Agent Builder -- create specialized AI agents with custom expertise and tool access\n- Workflow Builder -- design structured processes with steps and decision points\n- Module Builder -- package agents and workflows into shareable, publishable modules\n- Interactive setup with YAML configuration and npm publishing support\n\n## Creative Intelligence Suite\n\nAI-powered tools for structured creativity, ideation, and innovation during early-stage development. The suite provides multiple agents that facilitate brainstorming, design thinking, and problem-solving using proven frameworks.\n\n- **Code:** `cis`\n- **npm:** [`bmad-creative-intelligence-suite`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/bmad-creative-intelligence-suite)\n- **GitHub:** [bmad-code-org/bmad-module-creative-intelligence-suite](https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-module-creative-intelligence-suite)\n\n**Provides:**\n\n- Innovation Strategist, Design Thinking Coach, and Brainstorming Coach agents\n- Problem Solver and Creative Problem Solver for systematic and lateral thinking\n- Storyteller and Presentation Master for narratives and pitches\n- Ideation frameworks including SCAMPER, Reverse Brainstorming, and problem reframing\n\n## Game Dev Studio\n\nStructured game development workflows adapted for Unity, Unreal, Godot, and custom engines. Supports planning depths from rapid prototyping to full-scale production with epic-driven sprints; implementation converges on Build.\n\n- **Code:** `gds`\n- **npm:** [`bmad-game-dev-studio`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/bmad-game-dev-studio)\n- **GitHub:** [bmad-code-org/bmad-module-game-dev-studio](https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-module-game-dev-studio)\n\n**Provides:**\n\n- Game Design Document (GDD) generation workflow\n- Game-aware planning and context that feed the standard Build implementation loop\n- Narrative design support for characters, dialogue, and world-building\n- Coverage for 21+ game types with engine-specific architecture guidance\n\n## Test Architect (TEA)\n\nEnterprise-grade test strategy, automation guidance, and release gate decisions through an expert agent and nine structured workflows. TEA goes well beyond the built-in QA agent with risk-based prioritization and requirements traceability.\n\n- **Code:** `tea`\n- **npm:** [`bmad-method-test-architecture-enterprise`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/bmad-method-test-architecture-enterprise)\n- **GitHub:** [bmad-code-org/bmad-method-test-architecture-enterprise](https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-method-test-architecture-enterprise)\n\n**Provides:**\n\n- Murat agent (Master Test Architect and Quality Advisor)\n- Workflows for test design, ATDD, automation, test review, and traceability\n- NFR assessment, CI setup, and framework scaffolding\n- P0-P3 prioritization with optional Playwright Utils and MCP integrations\n\n## Community Modules\n\nCommunity modules and a module marketplace are coming. Check the [BMad GitHub organization](https://github.com/bmad-code-org) for updates.\n---\ntitle: 'How to Install BMad'\ndescription: Install, update, and pin BMad for local development, teams, and CI\nsidebar:\n  order: 1\n---\n\nUse `npx bmad-method install` to set up BMad in your project. One command handles first installs, upgrades, channel switching, and scripted CI runs. This page covers all of it.\n\n## When to Use This\n\n- Starting a new project with BMad\n- Adding or removing modules on an existing install\n- Switching a module to main-HEAD or pinning to a specific release\n- Scripting installs for CI pipelines, Dockerfiles, or enterprise rollouts\n\n:::note[Prerequisites]\n\n- **Node.js** 20.12+ (the installer requires it)\n- **Git** (for cloning external modules)\n- **An AI tool** such as Claude Code or Cursor (run `npx bmad-method install --list-tools` to see all supported tools)\n\n:::\n\n## First-time install (the fast path)\n\n```bash\nnpx bmad-method install\n```\n\nThe interactive flow asks you five things:\n\n1. Installation directory (defaults to the current working directory)\n2. Which modules to install (checkboxes for core, bmm, bmb, cis, gds, tea)\n3. **\"Ready to install (all stable)?\"** — Yes accepts the latest released tag for every external module\n4. Which AI tools/IDEs to integrate with (claude-code, cursor, and others)\n5. Per-module config (name, language, output folder)\n\nAccept the defaults and you land on the latest stable release of every module, configured for your chosen tool.\n\n:::tip[Just want the newest prerelease?]\n\n```bash\nnpx bmad-method@next install\n```\n\nRuns the prerelease installer, which ships a newer snapshot of core and bmm. More churn, fewer delays between development and release.\n:::\n\n## Picking a specific version\n\nTwo independent axes control what ends up on disk.\n\n### Axis 1: external module channels\n\nEvery external module — bmb, cis, gds, tea, and any community module — installs on one of three channels:\n\n| Channel            | What gets installed                                                          | Who picks this                          |\n| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |\n| `stable` (default) | Highest released semver tag. Prereleases like `v2.0.0-alpha.1` are excluded. | Most users                              |\n| `next`             | Main branch HEAD at install time                                             | Contributors, early adopters            |\n| `pinned`           | A specific tag you name                                                      | Enterprise installs, CI reproducibility |\n\nChannels are per-module. You can run bmb on `next` while leaving cis on `stable` — the flags below let you mix freely.\n\n### Axis 2: installer binary version\n\nThe `bmad-method` npm package itself has two dist-tags:\n\n| Command                               | What you get                                                      |\n| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| `npx bmad-method install` (`@latest`) | Latest stable installer release                                   |\n| `npx bmad-method@next install`        | Latest prerelease installer, auto-published on every push to main |\n\n**The installer binary determines your core and bmm versions.** Those two modules ship bundled inside the installer package rather than being cloned from separate repos.\n\n### Why core and bmm don't have their own channel\n\nThey're stapled to the installer binary you ran:\n\n- `npx bmad-method install` → latest stable core and bmm\n- `npx bmad-method@next install` → prerelease core and bmm\n- `node /path/to/local-checkout/tools/installer/bmad-cli.js install` → whatever your local checkout has\n\n`--pin bmm=v6.3.0` and `--next=bmm` are silently ineffective against bundled modules, and the installer warns you when you try. A future release extracts bmm from the installer package; once that ships, bmm gets a proper channel selector like bmb has today.\n\n## Updating an existing install\n\nRunning `npx bmad-method install` in a directory that already contains `_bmad/` gives you a menu:\n\n| Choice             | What it does                                                                                                                                                |\n| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| **Quick Update**   | Re-runs the install with your existing settings. Refreshes files, applies patches and minor stable upgrades, refuses major upgrades. Fast, non-interactive. |\n| **Modify Install** | Full interactive flow. Add or remove modules, reconfigure settings, optionally review and switch channels for existing modules.                             |\n\n### Upgrade prompts\n\nWhen Modify detects a newer stable tag for a module you've installed on `stable`, it classifies the diff and prompts accordingly:\n\n| Upgrade type | Example         | Default |\n| ------------ | --------------- | ------- |\n| Patch        | v1.7.0 → v1.7.1 | Y       |\n| Minor        | v1.7.0 → v1.8.0 | Y       |\n| Major        | v1.7.0 → v2.0.0 | **N**   |\n\nMajor defaults to N because breaking changes frequently surface as \"instability\" when they weren't expected. The prompt includes a GitHub release-notes URL so you can read what changed before accepting.\n\nUnder `--yes`, patch and minor upgrades apply automatically. Majors stay frozen — pass `--pin <code>=<new-tag>` to accept non-interactively.\n\n### Switching a module's channel\n\n**Interactively:** choose Modify → answer **Yes** to \"Review channel assignments?\" → each external module offers Keep, Switch to stable, Switch to next, or Pin to a tag.\n\n**Via flags:** the recipes in the next section cover the common cases.\n\n## Headless CI installs\n\n### Flag reference\n\n| Flag                                                                                       | Purpose                                                                                                                           |\n| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| `--yes`, `-y`                                                                              | Skip all prompts; accept flag values + defaults                                                                                   |\n| `--directory <path>`                                                                       | Install into this directory (default: current working dir)                                                                        |\n| `--modules <a,b,c>`                                                                        | Exact module set. Core is auto-added. Not a delta — list everything you want kept.                                                |\n| `--tools <a,b>`                                                                            | IDE/tool selection. Required for fresh `--yes` installs. Run `--list-tools` for valid IDs.                                        |\n| `--list-tools`                                                                             | Print all supported tool/IDE IDs (with target directories) and exit.                                                              |\n| `--action <type>`                                                                          | `install`, `update`, or `quick-update`. Defaults based on existing install state.                                                 |\n| `--custom-source <urls>`                                                                   | Install custom modules from Git URLs or local paths                                                                               |\n| `--channel <stable\\|next>`                                                                 | Apply to all externals (aliased as `--all-stable` / `--all-next`)                                                                 |\n| `--all-stable`                                                                             | Alias for `--channel=stable`                                                                                                      |\n| `--all-next`                                                                               | Alias for `--channel=next`                                                                                                        |\n| `--next=<code>`                                                                            | Put one module on next. Repeatable.                                                                                               |\n| `--pin <code>=<tag>`                                                                       | Pin one module to a specific tag. Repeatable.                                                                                     |\n| `--set <module>.<key>=<value>`                                                             | Set any module config option non-interactively (preferred — see [Module config overrides](#module-config-overrides)). Repeatable. |\n| `--list-options [module]`                                                                  | Print every `--set` key for built-in and locally-cached official modules, then exit. Pass a module code to scope to one module.   |\n| `--user-name`, `--communication-language`, `--document-output-language`, `--output-folder` | Legacy shortcuts equivalent to `--set core.<key>=<value>` (still supported)                                                       |\n\nPrecedence when flags overlap: `--pin` beats `--next=` beats `--channel` / `--all-*` beats the registry default (`stable`).\n\n:::note[Example resolution]\n`--all-next --pin cis=v0.2.0` puts bmb, gds, and tea on next while pinning cis to v0.2.0.\n:::\n\n### Recipes\n\n**Default install — latest stable for everything:**\n\n```bash\nnpx bmad-method install --yes --modules bmm,bmb,cis --tools claude-code\n```\n\n**Enterprise pin — reproducible byte-for-byte:**\n\n```bash\nnpx bmad-method install --yes \\\n  --modules bmm,bmb,cis \\\n  --pin bmb=v1.7.0 --pin cis=v0.2.0 \\\n  --tools claude-code\n```\n\n**Bleeding edge — externals on main HEAD:**\n\n```bash\nnpx bmad-method install --yes --modules bmm,bmb --all-next --tools claude-code\n```\n\n**Add a module to an existing install** (keep everything else):\n\n```bash\nnpx bmad-method install --yes --action update \\\n  --modules bmm,bmb,gds\n```\n\n`--tools` is omitted intentionally — `--action update` reuses the tools configured during the first install.\n\n**Mix channels — bmb on next, gds on stable:**\n\n```bash\nnpx bmad-method install --yes --action update \\\n  --modules bmm,bmb,cis,gds \\\n  --next=bmb\n```\n\n### Module config overrides\n\n`--set <module>.<key>=<value>` lets you set any module config option non-interactively. It's repeatable and scales to every module — present and future. The flag is applied as a post-install patch: the installer runs its normal flow first, then `--set` upserts each value into `_bmad/config.toml` (team scope) or `_bmad/config.user.toml` (user scope), and into `_bmad/<module>/config.yaml` so declared values carry forward to the next install.\n\n**Example — install bmm with explicit project knowledge and skill level:**\n\n```bash\nnpx bmad-method install --yes \\\n  --modules bmm \\\n  --tools claude-code \\\n  --set bmm.project_knowledge=research \\\n  --set bmm.user_skill_level=expert\n```\n\n**Discover available keys for a module:**\n\n```bash\nnpx bmad-method install --list-options bmm\n```\n\n`--list-options` (no argument) lists every key the installer can find locally — built-in modules (`core`, `bmm`) plus any currently cached official modules. The cache is per-machine and can be cleared, so previously installed officials won't appear on a fresh checkout or an ephemeral CI worker until they're installed again. Community and custom modules aren't enumerated here; read the module's `module.yaml` directly to see what keys it declares.\n\n**How it works:**\n\n- **Routing.** The patch step looks for `[modules.<module>] <key>` (or `[core] <key>`) in `config.user.toml` first; if found there, it updates that file. Otherwise it writes to the team-scope `config.toml`. So user-scope keys (e.g. `core.user_name`, `bmm.user_skill_level`) end up in `config.user.toml` and team-scope keys end up in `config.toml`, matching the partition the installer uses.\n- **Verbatim values.** The value is written exactly as you provided it — no `result:` template rendering. To get the rendered form (e.g. `{project-root}/research`), pass it explicitly: `--set bmm.project_knowledge='{project-root}/research'`.\n- **Carry-forward, declared keys.** Values for keys declared in `module.yaml` survive subsequent installs because they're also written to `_bmad/<module>/config.yaml`, which the installer reads as the prompt default on the next run.\n- **Carry-forward, undeclared keys.** A value for a key the module's schema doesn't declare lands in `config.toml` for the current install but won't be re-emitted on the next install (the manifest writer's schema-strict partition drops unknown keys). Re-pass `--set` if you need it sticky, or edit `_bmad/config.toml` directly.\n- **No validation.** `single-select` values aren't checked against the allowed choices, and unknown keys aren't rejected — whatever you assert is written.\n- **Modules not in `--modules`.** Setting a value for a module you didn't include prints a warning and the value is dropped (no file gets created for an uninstalled module).\n\nThe legacy core shortcuts (`--user-name`, `--output-folder`, etc.) still work and remain documented for backward compatibility, but `--set core.user_name=...` is equivalent.\n\n:::note[Works with quick-update]\n`--set` is a post-install patch, so it applies the same way regardless of action type. Under `bmad install --action quick-update` (or `--yes` against an existing install, where quick-update is the default), `--set` patches the central config files at the end just like a regular install.\n:::\n\n:::caution[Rate limit on shared IPs]\nAnonymous GitHub API calls are capped at 60/hour per IP. A single install hits the API once per external module to resolve the stable tag. Offices behind NAT, CI runner pools, and VPNs can collectively exhaust this.\n\nSet `GITHUB_TOKEN=<personal access token>` in the environment to raise the limit to 5000/hour per account. Any public-repo-read PAT works; no scopes are required.\n:::\n\n## What got installed\n\nAfter any install, `_bmad/_config/manifest.yaml` records exactly what's on disk:\n\n```yaml\nmodules:\n  - name: bmb\n    version: v1.7.0 # the tag, or \"main\" for next\n    channel: stable # stable | next | pinned\n    sha: 86033fc9aeae2ca6d52c7cdb675c1f4bf17fc1c1\n    source: external\n    repoUrl: https://github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-builder\n```\n\nThe `sha` field is written for git-backed modules (external, community, and URL-based custom). Bundled modules (core, bmm) and local-path custom modules don't have one — their code travels with the installer binary or your filesystem, not a cloneable ref.\n\nFor cross-machine reproducibility, don't rely on rerunning the same `--modules` command. Stable-channel installs resolve to the highest released tag **at install time**, so a later rerun lands on whatever has been released since. Convert the recorded tags from `manifest.yaml` into explicit `--pin` flags on the target machine, e.g.:\n\n```bash\nnpx bmad-method install --yes --modules bmb,cis \\\n  --pin bmb=v1.7.0 --pin cis=v0.4.2 --tools claude-code\n```\n\n## Troubleshooting\n\n### \"Could not resolve stable tag\" or \"API rate limit exceeded\"\n\nYou've hit GitHub's 60/hr anonymous limit. Set `GITHUB_TOKEN` and retry. If you already have a token set, it may be expired or rate-limited on its own budget — try a different token or wait for the hourly reset.\n\n### \"Tag 'vX.Y.Z' not found\"\n\nThe tag you passed to `--pin` doesn't exist in the module's repo. Check the repo's releases page on GitHub for valid tags.\n\n### A pinned install keeps upgrading\n\nPinned installs don't upgrade. Quick-update applies patches and minors on stable channel only; it won't touch `pinned` or `next`. If a pinned install changed, open `_bmad/_config/manifest.yaml` — `channel: pinned` plus a fixed `version` and `sha` should hold across runs unless you explicitly override via flags.\n\n### `--pin bmm=X` didn't do anything\n\nbmm is a bundled module — `--pin` and `--next=` don't apply. Use `npx bmad-method@next install` for a prerelease core/bmm, or check out the bmad-bmm repo and run the installer locally to get unreleased changes.\n"
  }
]

When two currently-live sources or companions disagree on the same field, or an either/or never got resolved, surface it to the user rather than silently choosing — the resolution is itself a new memlog entry.\n\nIf the input is genuinely too thin to distill (e.g. \"an app for hikers\" with no surrounding context), stop and suggest `bmad-prd` (or sibling ceremony skill). Companions follow the same lean discipline as SPEC.md (Spec Law rule 8).\n\n**Spawn a companion when the content needs more than one kernel-shape line:** multi-item catalogs (per-entity matrices like archetypes, drinks, modes, routes), tables, diagrams (always), editorial voice rules, long-form reference material the kernel cites by name (glossary, brownfield notes, project conventions). The originating skill owns them.\n\nTwo rules govern companions:\n\n1. **Name spec-authored companions for the content type they hold.** `glossary.md`, `<entity-class>.md` (e.g. `patron-archetypes.md`, `medication-routes.md`, `flight-modes.md`), `stack.md`, `conventions.md`, `brownfield.md`, `architecture-diagrams.md`, `state-machines.md`, `failure-modes.md`, `compliance-references.md`. The operation aims for them; the self-validate sweep enforces them.\n\n1. **Each capability has both `intent` and `success`.** Missing either = not a capability.\n2. **Intents describe WHAT, not HOW.** Implementation prescription belongs in a companion (stack, conventions).\n3. **Constraints actually bend design decisions.** A \"constraint\" that rules nothing out is decoration.\n4. **Non-goals are explicit.** At least one. Wrapper ceremony does not.\n8. **Lean prose.** Every sentence carries load-bearing content. Cut decoration, hedges, backstory, throat-clearing. Applies to SPEC.md, companions, and `.memlog.md`.\n\n## Self-Validate\n\nAfter every create or update, sweep the resulting artifact in **two passes** before presenting.\n\n**Pass 1 — Coherence.** Judge the spec against Spec Law rules 1–6 and 8. For anything that fails or feels weak, attempt to fix it without inventing content the input did not support. Calls made without direct confirmation become `assumptions[]`; gaps that could not be filled become `open_questions[]`.\n\n**Pass 2 — Preservation.** Walk the source claim by claim. Confirm each load-bearing claim landed in SPEC.md or a companion. Wrapper-ceremony drops are logged under \"Wrapper-only content\" so the drop is on the record, not silent.\n\nRecord the verdict for each pass to `.memlog.md` (`append --type event`). The update itself never rewrites `stories.yaml`.\n\nEither way, walk the capabilities and constraints with the user and propose a story per independently reviewable slice — this is a conversation, not a silent render. Never list it in `companions:` and never point a frontmatter key at it: companions carry the what-to-build contract every consumer reads; `stories.yaml` is input for whichever tool dispatches the stories.\n\nField definitions, the validity rules, and a worked example live in `assets/stories-schema.md`. Before writing or re-writing the file, check every entry against those rules; fix violations rather than presenting a file that fails them. Record the check's verdict to `.memlog.md` (`append --type event`), the same discipline as Self-Validate.\n\nDerive `stories.yaml` from `.memlog.md` exactly like any other spec-authored artifact: log each proposed story (`--type decision`) as the user agrees to it, then render. On a later run against the same spec folder, re-derive the same way, handling ids per the schema's update semantics.\n\n## Output\n\n**Interactive** — share the spec folder path conversationally. Name the capability count, the companions produced, and the verdict in one or two sentences. Name the story count too if `stories.yaml` was written this run. If `assumptions[]` or `open_questions[]` are non-empty, list them (short — one line each) and invite the user to walk through them. Make clear that addressing them can update the source input (if it was a file), the spec, or both — whichever combination the user prefers. Do not dump JSON or present a wall of output.\n\n**Headless** — return JSON per `assets/headless-schemas.md`.\n\nRun `{workflow.on_complete}` if set.\n\n## After Spec is Output\n\nAny update to the spec — resolved assumptions, answered open questions, other changes — is appended to `.memlog.md` as it happens. When a change overrides something that came from a source input, offer to update that source too, so upstream and the spec don't silently diverge.\n\n## Frontmatter conventions\n\n- `companions:` array of `.md` files downstream MUST read alongside SPEC.md to have the full contract. The split between spec-authored and adopted is implicit by path; downstream treats both the same.\n- `sources:` array of paths to files that were **fully absorbed** into the SPEC, with no remaining downstream value (e.g., a PRD whose every load-bearing claim is now in the kernel). Listed for audit and for bmad-spec to re-read on update. Downstream does NOT read these. Files that downstream still needs to read belong in `companions:`, not here.\n- **Do not list** the memlog, README files, organizational artifacts, or any operational record of how upstream skills produced their artifacts. You review and we iterate. The initial quality depends on how much you gave me upfront.\n- **Coaching path** — we walk PM-thinking sections together. Once chosen, I ask which entry point fits: **Vision + Features** (capability-first — for enterprise, dev products, internal tools, anyone who thinks in features), **Journey-led** (user-first — for consumer, UX-heavy, multi-stakeholder products; journeys with named protagonists carry persona context inline, no standalone persona section), or *let me suggest* based on what I heard. Reorder and combine for readability. Never include a section because it appears; never skip a concern because no template section covered it. Map\ndescription  | Visual reference for BMad Method workflow phases and outputs\nsidebar  | \norder\n1\n\nThe BMad Method (BMM) is a module in the BMad Ecosystem, targeted at following the best practices of context engineering and planning. AI agents work best with clear, structured context. The BMM system builds that context progressively across 4 distinct phases - each phase, and multiple workflows optionally within each phase, produce documents that inform the next, so agents always know what to build and why.\n\nThe rationale and concepts come from agile methodologies that have been used across the industry with great success as a mental framework.\n\nIf at any time you are unsure what to do, the `bmad-help` skill will help you stay on track or know what to do next. You can always refer to this for reference also - but `bmad-help` is fully interactive and much quicker if you have already installed the BMad Method. Additionally, if you are using different modules that have extended the BMad Method or added other complementary non-extension modules - `bmad-help` evolves to know all that is available to give you the best in-the-moment advice.\nNeither skill requires the other — start with `bmad-prd` directly if you already know what you're building. :::\n\n## Phase 3: Solutioning\n\nDecide how to build it and break work into stories.\n\nWorkflow  | Purpose  | Produces\n--- | --- | ---\n`bmad-architecture`  | Make technical decisions explicit  | `ARCHITECTURE-SPINE.md` is the spine by default but can hydrate to your desired output or presentation needs also\n`bmad-create-epics-and-stories`  | Break requirements into implementable work  | Epic files with stories\n`bmad-check-implementation-readiness`  | Gate check before implementation  | PASS/CONCERNS/FAIL decision\n\n## Phase 4: Implementation\n\nBuild it, one story at a time. Phase 4 epic and story automation is now available also. So you can choose how you want to stay in the loop. You can choose the full flow, or go right to quick flow.\n\nWorkflow  | Purpose  | Produces\n--- | --- | ---\n`bmad-sprint-planning`  | Initialize tracking (once per project to sequence the dev cycle)  | `sprint-status.yaml`\n`bmad-create-story`  | Prepare next story for implementation  | `story-[slug].md`\n`bmad-dev-story`  | Implement the story  | Working code + tests\n`bmad-code-review`  | Validate implementation quality  | Approved or changes requested\n`bmad-correct-course`  | Handle significant mid-sprint changes  | Updated plan or re-routing\n`bmad-sprint-status`  | Track sprint progress and story status  | Sprint status update\n`bmad-retrospective`  | Review after epic completion  | Lessons learned\n\n## Quick Flow (Parallel Track)\n\nSkip phases 1-3 for small, well-understood work.\n\nWorkflow  | Purpose  | Produces\n--- | --- | ---\n`bmad-quick-dev`  | Unified quick flow — clarify intent, plan, implement, review, and present  | `spec-*.md` + code\n`bmad-dev-auto`  | Runs one unattended development-loop iteration — small intent in, code out  | `spec-*.md` + code\n\nFor the reference on unattended development loops with `bmad-dev-auto`, see Autonomous Development Loops.\n\n## Context Management\n\nEach document becomes context for the next phase. The PRD tells the architect what constraints matter. The architecture tells the dev agent which patterns to follow. Story files give focused, complete context for implementation. Without this structure, agents make inconsistent decisions.\n\n### Project Context\n\n:::tip[Recommended] Create `project-context.md` to ensure AI agents follow your project's rules and preferences. This file works like a constitution for your project — it guides implementation decisions across all workflows. This optional file can be generated at the end of Architecture Creation, or in an existing project it can be generated also to capture whats important to keep aligned with current conventions. :::\n\nHow to create it:\n\n  * Manually — Create `_bmad-output/project-context.md` with your technology stack and implementation rules\n  * Generate it — Run `bmad-generate-project-context` to auto-generate from your architecture or codebase\n\nLearn more about project-context.md\n\nYou can’t perform that action at this time.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------\nReleases · bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD · GitHub (https://github.com/bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/releases)\nciteturn5search2 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 2 months ago; # Releases: bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD ... Otherwise, generate it after architecture to capture those decisions. :::\n\n## What Goes In It\n\nThe file has two main sections:\n\n### Technology Stack & Versions\n\nDocuments the frameworks, languages, and tools your project uses with specific versions:\n    \n    ## Technology Stack & Versions\n    \n    - Node.js 20.x, TypeScript 5.3, React 18.2\n    - State: Zustand (not Redux)\n    - Testing: Vitest, Playwright, MSW\n    - Styling: Tailwind CSS with custom design tokens\n\n### Critical Implementation Rules\n\nDocuments patterns and conventions that agents might otherwise miss:\n\nWithout Context  | With Context\n--- | ---\nUses generic patterns  | Follows your established conventions\nInconsistent style across stories  | Consistent implementation\nMay miss project-specific constraints  | Respects all technical requirements\nEach agent decides independently  | All agents align with same rules\n\nThis is especially important for:\n\n  * Quick Flow — skips PRD and architecture, so context file fills the gap\n  * Team projects — ensures all agents follow the same standards\n  * Existing projects — prevents breaking established patterns\n\n## Editing and Updating\n\nThe `project-context.md` file is a living document. Update it when:\n\n  * Architecture decisions change\n  * New conventions are established\n  * Patterns evolve during implementation\n  * You identify gaps from agent behavior\n\nYou can edit it manually at any time, or re-run `bmad-generate-project-context` to update it after significant changes.\n\n:::note[File Location] The default location is `_bmad-output/project-context.md`. Workflows search for it there, and also check `**/project-context.md` anywhere in your project. :::\n--------------------------------------------------------------------------------\nBMAD-METHOD/docs/tutorials/getting-started.md at main · bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD · GitHub (https://github.com/bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/blob/main/docs/tutorials/getting-started.md)\nciteturn5search5 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 2 months ago; 3  | Solutioning  | Design architecture (BMad Method/Enterprise only) ... Quick Flow  | Bug fixes, simple features, clear scope (1-15 stories)  | Tech-spec only\n## Understanding BMad\n\nBMad helps you build software through guided workflows with specialized AI agents. The process follows four phases:\n\nPhase  | Name  | What Happens\n--- | --- | ---\n1  | Analysis  | Brainstorming, research, product brief or PRFAQ (optional)\n2  | Planning  | Create requirements (PRD or spec)\n3  | Solutioning  | Design architecture (BMad Method/Enterprise only)\n4  | Implementation  | Build epic by epic, story by story\n\nOpen the Workflow Map to explore phases, workflows, and context management.\n\nBased on your project's complexity, BMad offers three planning tracks:\n\nTrack  | Best For  | Documents Created\n--- | --- | ---\nQuick Flow  | Bug fixes, simple features, clear scope (1-15 stories)  | Tech-spec only\nBMad Method  | Products, platforms, complex features (10-50+ stories)  | PRD + Architecture + UX\nEnterprise  | Compliance, multi-tenant systems (30+ stories)  | PRD + Architecture + Security + DevOps\n\n:::note Story counts are guidance, not definitions. You can even do it during or after a project to help keep docs up to date.\n\n### Can I use Quick Flow for established projects?\n\nSection titled “Can I use Quick Flow for established projects?”\n\nYes! Quick Flow works great for established projects. It will:\n\n  * Auto-detect your existing stack\n  * Analyze existing code patterns\n  * Detect conventions and ask for confirmation\n  * Generate context-rich spec that respects existing code\n\nPerfect for bug fixes and small features in existing codebases.\n\n### What if my existing code doesn’t follow best practices?\n\nSection titled “What if my existing code doesn’t follow best practices?”\n\nQuick Flow detects your conventions and asks: “Should I follow these existing conventions?” You decide:\n\n  * Yes → Maintain consistency with current codebase\n  * No → Establish new standards (document why in spec)\n\nBMM respects your choice — it won’t force modernization, but it will offer it.\n--------------------------------------------------------------------------------\nBMad Method Workflow Map (https://docs.bmad-method.org/workflow-map-diagram.html)\nciteturn5search9 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; Please reload this page.\nL194: \nL195: ## No results found\nL196: \nL197: cite76†View all tags L198: \nL199: cite77†Image: @github-actions†avatars.githubusercontent.com cite78†github-actions released this 03 Jul 23:57\nL200: \nL201: cite66†v6.10.0 L202: \nL203: cite79†`081e64e` L204: ### ✨ Headline\nL205: bmad-loop lands as an installable module, and the automator that came before it steps aside. bmad-loop — the successor project for unattended dev-loop orchestration, adversarial review, and deferred-work sweeps — is now selectable straight from the installer picker, driven by the new bmad-dev-auto skill: a single-iteration unattended worker that clarifies intent, creates or resumes a spec, implements, reviews, and finalizes, all off a spec-frontmatter state machine an orchestrator can poll.\nL206: bmad-automator, the experimental predecessor, is now deprecated in its favor.\nL207: Also in this release: party-mode gets an anti-consensus room and two sync fixes, the code-review/edge-case-hunter pipeline gets sharper severity triage and a named-set generalization pass, and bmad-investigate is retired.\nL208: ### 💥 Breaking Changes\nL209: \nL210:   * bmad-automator deprecated, replaced by bmad-loop (cite80†#2532 ). New installs no longer show BMad Automator in the picker. Existing installs are untouched and keep showing, with a migration hint pointing to BMad Loop. If you're on Automator, plan the move to `bmad-loop`.\nL211: ### 🎁 Features\nL212:   * bmad-loop — new marketplace module (cite80†#2532 ). BMad's unattended-dev orchestrator ships as an opt-in installer module (`bmad-loop`, not selected by default). Its skills live behind a `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` rather than a normal `module.yaml` folder, so the installer gained a `marketplace-plugin` registry flag that routes it through the existing custom-plugin resolver, and now fails loudly instead of installing an empty module if resolution comes up short.\nL213: Installing the module only stages files — finish setup by running the `bmad-loop-setup` skill, which installs the orchestrator and wires up per-project hooks and policy; automation doesn't run until that completes. A new `post-install-message` registry field surfaces this instruction right after install (blocking on interactive installs so it isn't missed, non-blocking with `--yes`).\nL214:   * bmad-dev-auto — new unattended workflow skill (cite81†#2500 and nine follow-ups). A Quick Dev sibling built to keep moving without a human in the loop, driven entirely off spec-frontmatter status so an orchestrator like bmad-loop can poll it.\nL215: Hardened through the release: an append-only review-triage log with loopback tracking (cite82†#2505 ); an end-of-run commit so the worktree stays clean into the next iteration (cite83†#2506 ); a fix to the Blind Hunter reviewer, which was wrongly denied project access (\"blind\" means blind to intent, not to the codebase) (cite84†#2507 ); re-entry on a completed spec to trigger a fresh follow-up review pass (cite85†#2508 ); a `final_revision` recorded in frontmatter at exit, the only link back from an out-of-tree spec to its in-tree commits (cite86†#2522 ); a closed gap where Finalize could leave `status: draft` on an otherwise-done run (cite87†#2536 ); and a hardened contract requiring subagents to be invoked synchronously, since there's no event loop to resume a yielded turn (cite88†#2543 ).\nL216: Reference doc at `docs/reference/dev-auto.md` (cite89†#2519 ), retitled \"Autonomous Development Loops\" (cite90†#2521 ). Some of the same prompt fixes were backported to Quick Dev (cite91†#2501 ).\nL217:   * party-mode: anti-consensus club (cite92†#2530 ). New built-in persona group (Wildcard, Level, Killjoy, Splinter) for decision rooms that resist fast agreement while keeping a human in control. Launch with `--party=anti-concensus-club`, and use `--mode subagent` for best results. These can be configured as defaults if you use bmad customize and specify that.\nL218:   * Two new elicitation methods: Subtraction and Map Is Not the Territory (cite93†#2515 ). Subtraction counters additive bias; Map Is Not the Territory guards against over-trusting a lossy model.\nL219:   * Edge Case Hunter: named-set generalization pass (cite94†#2524 ). Catches diffs that special-case some members of a fixed set (enum, status code, sentinel, flag) while leaving the rest as silent unhandled branches. Measured catch-rate improvement of 50% to 100% on a real regression, at a 19% token cost per run.\nL220: ### 🐛 Fixes\nL221:   * party-mode stays interactive and the room stays in sync (cite95†#2531 ). Fixes a bug, observed under Codex, where a runtime treated the opening prompt as one-shot and closed spawned agents once satisfied. Party mode is open-ended by default now, ending only on explicit signal, with an opt-in `--non-interactive` flag; standing agents are kept alive and resumed rather than dropped.\nL222:   * party-mode: agent-team sync corrected to point-to-point (cite96†#2539 ). Claude Code Agent Teams communicate mailbox-style, not over a shared broadcast channel, so an idle member doesn't see exchanges it isn't addressed in. Docs updated so the lead relays turns; subagent mode, which is genuinely broadcast, is unchanged.\nL223:   * Code-review triage severity calibration hardened (cite97†#2523 ). Requires reading surrounding source (call sites, guards) before rating severity instead of judging from the diff hunk alone, fixing over-rated unreachable findings, and drops a \"prefer conservative when uncertain\" tie-breaker that was inflating severity.\nL224:   * Deletion audit folded into Edge Case Hunter (cite98†#2525 ). Retires the standalone deletion-contract auditor layer, which added cold-start cost for near-zero yield, in favor of a gated deletion check inside Edge Case Hunter's existing turn.\nL225:   * Review layer invocation normalized (cite99†#2526 ). Removes stale \"no access/control\" wording from code-review/quick-dev/dev-auto prompts and normalizes Blind Hunter / Edge Case Hunter invocation phrasing.\nL226:   * Installer accepts Windows custom module paths (cite100†#2511 ). Local paths like `C:\\modules\\foo`, `C:/modules/foo`, and `.\\foo` no longer fall through to the Git-URL parser and get rejected.\nL227:   * bmad-help reads central config (cite101†#2541 ). Its config data source now goes through the shared four-layer TOML resolver instead of legacy `config.yaml`/`user-config.yaml`, fixing `communication_language` and `project_knowledge` not reaching the skill.\nL228: ### 📚 Docs\nL229: \nL230:   * bmad-forge-idea wording tightened (cite102†#2513 ). Overview, session, persona, and exit language rewritten more directly; no behavior change.\nL231:   * validate-skills exempts deprecated skills from the trigger-phrase check (cite103†#2486 ). Thin compatibility shims (`bmad-create-prd`, `bmad-edit-prd`, `bmad-validate-prd`, `bmad-create-architecture`) intentionally omit a trigger phrase to steer users to their replacement.\nL232: ### 🗑️ Removed\nL233: \nL234:   * bmad-investigate retired. It reached the same conclusions as plain investigation at higher cost; the case-file artifact didn't justify the overhead.\nL235: \nL236: Assets 2\nL237: \nL238: Loading\nL239: \nL240: ### Uh oh!\nL241: \nL242: There was an error while loading.
